entries.name: Melrose Wang Capital Investments LLC v. Houston Hotel Partners, LLC

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Plaintiff's contention that Section 8.3 should be read in isolation, without reference back to Sections 8.1 and 8.2: rejected. The Court agreed with the Report's reading that "any such Manager or Member" incorporates the Section 8.1/8.2 eligibility criteria.

Advancement under Section 8.3 read standalone: rejected in the alternative. The affirmative Plenary Action does not relate to Plaintiff's "involvement with the Company," and the standard-of-conduct statement and repayment undertaking make no sense where the underlying proceeding does not concern the claimant's conduct; the Court quoted with approval the Company's brief on this point.

authorities_cited.authority: Operating Agreement §§ 8.1, 8.2, 8.3
authorities_cited.proposition: Advancement under § 8.3 extends to "any such Manager or Member," read with the §§ 8.1–8.2 indemnification and exculpation criteria (acts in good faith on behalf of the Company), in actions relating to the Member's involvement with the Company, subject to a standard-of-conduct statement and repayment undertaking.

authorities_cited.authority: DiGiacobbe v. Sestak, 743 A.2d 180 (Del. 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: The Court reviews a Magistrate's determinations de novo on exceptions.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Est. of Erdman, 2011 WL 2191680 (Del. Ch. May 26, 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: A report is adopted where the decision is supported by the factual record and its conclusions of law are proper.

summary.brief_summary: Melrose Wang Capital Investments LLC, a member of Houston Hotel Partners, LLC, sought advancement under Operating Agreement § 8.3 for its own plenary suit alleging that the Company and AAFF made distributions in breach of the waterfall. The Magistrate in Chancery recommended denial, and Plaintiff took exceptions. Vice Chancellor David, reviewing de novo, adopted the Report. The Court added that, even on Plaintiff's standalone reading of § 8.3, an affirmative member suit challenging others' conduct is not a proceeding relating to the Member's involvement with the Company, as the standard-of-conduct conditions confirm.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether Section 8.3 of the Company's Operating Agreement, which mandates advancement for a Member in an action "relating to" the Member's "involvement with the Company" upon a good-faith statement and repayment undertaking, entitles a Member to advancement of expenses in its own affirmative suit against the Company and another member for breach of the Operating Agreement's distribution waterfall.
summary.holding: Exceptions denied; the Magistrate's Report is adopted and affirmed. On de novo review, the Court agreed with the Report that Section 8.3 advancement is available only to a Member eligible for indemnification or exculpation under Sections 8.1 or 8.2, and that Plaintiff is not acting on behalf of the Company in the Plenary Action. Independently, even reading Section 8.3 in isolation, the Court held that Plaintiff's affirmative claims do not relate to Plaintiff's "involvement with the Company," except insofar as Plaintiff has standing to challenge the board's and AAFF's conduct. The Court reasoned that Section 8.3's standard-of-conduct statement and repayment undertaking do not make sense for a proceeding that does not concern the claimant's conduct.
key_facts_and_concessions: Plaintiff is a member of the Company, a Delaware LLC, and is the plaintiff, not a defendant, in the Plenary Action (C.A. No. 2025-1262-BWD) against the Company and another member, AAFF.

The Plenary Action alleges the Company and AAFF breached the Operating Agreement by directing and approving distributions to AAFF in violation of the waterfall provisions and by amending or modifying the Operating Agreement without Plaintiff's consent; it seeks damages and a declaration that Sections 4.3 and 6.3 do not provide an alternative to the waterfall.

Section 8.3 requires advancement for "any such Manager or Member" in an action "relating to Manager or Member's involvement with the Company," conditioned on a written statement of good-faith belief that the applicable standard of conduct was met and an undertaking to repay if it is determined that it was not.

Sections 8.1 and 8.2 indemnify and exculpate Members and Managers only for acts performed in good faith "on behalf of the Company" and reasonably believed to be within the authority conferred by the Operating Agreement.

The Magistrate's June 25, 2026 oral Report concluded that "any such Manager or Member" in Section 8.3 refers back to those eligible under Sections 8.1 or 8.2, and that Plaintiff is not acting "on behalf of the Company" within the scope of its authority in the Plenary Action.

The Court found that the Plenary Action does not concern Plaintiff's conduct and relates to Plaintiff's involvement with the Company only insofar as Plaintiff has standing to challenge the board's and AAFF's conduct.
summary.practical_takeaway: Advancement provisions keyed to a claimant's standard of conduct and a repayment undertaking will likely be read to cover defense of claims about the claimant's own conduct, not a member's affirmative suit to enforce distribution rights. Members who want fee-shifting for enforcement suits should bargain for an express prevailing-party or enforcement-fee clause.
summary.standard_of_review: De novo review of the Magistrate in Chancery's factual and legal determinations on exceptions (DiGiacobbe v. Sestak).

entries.name: Phil Mezey v. Synergy Thermogen, Inc.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Mezey's contention that the Underlying Action claims arise "by reason of the fact" of his agreement to serve as a Synergy director: rejected; under the Fourth Amended Petition no Synergy corporate powers were used or necessary for the alleged misconduct.

Treating the Fourth Amended Petition as a mere relabeling that cannot defeat advancement: rejected; the amendment substantively changed the claims by removing the director-based counts, so this was not a cosmetic attempt to plead around advancement.
Reliance on the prior petitions' references to Mezey as a "board member": rejected; the Court examines the underlying conduct, not the label attached to the role.

Fiduciary duty claim as covered: rejected; the duties arise from the advisory relationship and personal undertakings to provide business advice, which are distinct from his agreement to serve as a director.
Tortious interference claim as covered: rejected; it arises from withholding commercial support and has no connection to his agreement to serve on the board.

Alter ego, fraud and negligent misrepresentation claims as covered: rejected; they arise from commercial dealings and entity obligations, and imposing them on Mezey through ownership and control does not link them to his director agreement.
Conspiracy claim as covered: rejected; it concerns the same business conduct as the other claims.
Synergy's motion to dismiss for laches or to stay: not reached because of the summary judgment recommendation (fn. 66).

authorities_cited.authority: Synergy Certificate of Incorporation art. VI, §§ A, C
authorities_cited.proposition: Mandatory indemnification and advancement (upon an undertaking) for anyone made a party "by reason of the fact" that the person is, was or has agreed to become a director or officer.

authorities_cited.authority: Synergy Bylaws art. VII, § 7.02
authorities_cited.proposition: Indemnification and advancement for Covered Persons made parties by reason of the fact that they are or were a director or officer.

authorities_cited.authority: Homestore, Inc. v. Tafeen, 888 A.2d 204 (Del. 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: "By reason of the fact" requires a nexus or causal connection between the underlying proceeding and the official corporate capacity, without regard to motivation.

authorities_cited.authority: Bernstein v. TractManager, Inc., 953 A.2d 1003 (Del. Ch. 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: The nexus is established if corporate powers were used or necessary for the commission of the alleged misconduct.

authorities_cited.authority: Weaver v. ZeniMax Media, Inc., 2004 WL 243163 (Del. Ch. Jan. 30, 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: "By reason of the fact" is not construed so broadly as to cover every suit against a director; claims about personal obligations fall outside it.

authorities_cited.authority: Alalfi Fam. Tr. v. Cohen, 2020 WL 13854374 (Del. Ch. Feb. 19, 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: "By reason of the fact" is interpreted broadly and in favor of advancement.

authorities_cited.authority: Carr v. Glob. Payments Inc., 2019 WL 6726214 (Del. Ch. Dec. 11, 2019)
authorities_cited.proposition: Parties may eliminate advancement obligations by amending claims, which can moot the dispute, but mere relabeling of substantially unchanged claims will not suffice and draws skepticism.

authorities_cited.authority: Barr v. Genesis CMG Hldgs., LLC, 2025 WL 3720720 (Del. Ch. Dec. 23, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: The court looks to substance over form; a corporation may moot advancement by removing the claims that trigger the right.

authorities_cited.authority: Brown v. LiveOps, Inc., 903 A.2d 324 (Del. Ch. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: It would be inequitable to allow evasion of advancement through cosmetic amendments that leave the claim essentially unaltered.

authorities_cited.authority: Keller v. Steep Hill, Inc., 2023 WL 5624215 (Del. Ch. Aug. 31, 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Courts focus on the conduct underlying a claim, not its label.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 56(f)
authorities_cited.proposition: The June 2026 amendment makes explicit that the Court may grant summary judgment for a nonmovant.

authorities_cited.authority: Sun-Times Media Gp. v. Black, 954 A.2d 380 (Del. Ch. 2008)
authorities_cited.proposition: The Court may grant summary judgment for the nonmoving party when denying the movant's motion.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 56(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment standard; per fn. 30, the amended rule intends no substantive change and prior Delaware authorities remain applicable.

authorities_cited.authority: Rhodes v. bioMerieux, Inc., 2024 WL 669034 (Del. Ch. Feb. 19, 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment suits advancement disputes; plain meaning of the advancement provisions governs.

authorities_cited.authority: Senior Tour Players 207 Mgmt. Co. LLC v. Golftown 207 Hldg. Co., LLC, 853 A.2d 124 (Del. Ch. 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: Advancement turns on the corporate instruments and the underlying pleadings.

authorities_cited.authority: Mooney v. Echo Therapeutics, Inc., 2015 WL 3413272 (Del. Ch. May 28, 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited through Carr for the power to eliminate advancement by amending claims.

authorities_cited.authority: Xu Hong Bin v. Heckmann Corp., 2010 WL 187018 (Del. Ch. Jan. 8, 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: A corporation avoided advancement by representing it is not pursuing and will not pursue certain claims.
Referenced in the Certificate and Bylaws as the measure of indemnification "to the fullest extent permitted."
Basis of Synergy's laches dismissal or stay motion, which was not reached.
Final Report procedure and the deadline for exceptions.

summary.brief_summary: Phil Mezey, a Blackbrush principal sued by Synergy Thermogen, Inc. in the Texas Business Court, sought advancement under Synergy's Certificate and Bylaws and moved for summary judgment, while Synergy moved to dismiss on laches grounds or to stay; a Magistrate in Chancery issued a Final Report. The Court held that Mezey's agreement to become a director was a covered capacity, but that Synergy's post-filing Fourth Amended Petition genuinely eliminated the director-based counts. The remaining claims target his advisory and commercial conduct, which required no use of Synergy corporate powers, so the Court recommended summary judgment for Synergy and did not reach laches or stay.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether a Blackbrush principal who agreed (but never actually served) to become a Synergy director, a covered capacity under Synergy's Certificate, was entitled to mandatory advancement for the Texas Underlying Action, where Synergy's Fourth Amended Petition, filed after the advancement action began, dropped the counts premised on his agreement to serve and the remaining claims target his advisory and commercial conduct, so the question was whether those claims arise "by reason of the fact" of his agreement to become a director.
summary.holding: Final Report recommends that Mezey's motion be denied and summary judgment be granted in favor of nonmovant Synergy. The Court found that Mezey's agreement to become a director (February 2021 letter; BMAA) is a covered capacity under the Certificate's plain language. However, the Fourth Amended Petition substantively, not cosmetically, removed the director-based promissory estoppel and statutory fraud counts. Each remaining claim (fiduciary duty, tortious interference, alter ego, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, conspiracy) arises from Mezey's advisory relationship and the parties' commercial dealings, not from any use of Synergy corporate powers. No claim therefore arises "by reason of the fact" of his agreement to serve, and Synergy has no advancement obligation under its Certificate or Bylaws. Synergy's laches and stay motion was not reached (fn. 66). Notices of exceptions are due by October 27, 2026.
key_facts_and_concessions: After Mezey filed this advancement action, Synergy filed the Fourth Amended Petition, removing the promissory estoppel and statutory fraud counts that the Third Amended Petition had based on Mezey's agreement to serve as a director.

Mezey concedes he never actually served as a Synergy director or received board-level information entrusted to Synergy directors (Mezey Dep. 229); per the Court, he was never appointed, invited to a board meeting or given information customarily provided to a new board member.

Mezey agreed to become a director in a February 2021 letter to prospective investors ("will provide leadership on the board of directors") and under the June 10, 2021 BMAA (§§ 1, 7(a)), entered into by a special purpose LLC that Mezey and others formed; Synergy's board approved the BMAA by written consent.

The Certificate (art. VI, §§ A, C) mandates indemnification and advancement for anyone who "is or was, or has agreed to become, a director or officer"; the Court held Mezey's agreement to serve was a covered capacity.
The remaining fiduciary duty claim alleges Mezey owed duties as a "trusted business advisor[]" under the BMAA and Texas law, based on his oil and gas expertise and financing and customer assurances.

The other remaining claims (tortious interference, alter ego, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, conspiracy) concern withheld commercial support, entity defendants' financing and deployment obligations, and misuse of Synergy's technology, equipment and information.

Mezey's March 30, 2026 demand included a written undertaking to repay; Synergy rejected it on April 17, 2026, asserting among other grounds that Mezey was never formally appointed and that the claims did not arise "by reason of the fact" of his status.

Synergy did not move for summary judgment; it moved under Ct. Ch. R. 12(b)(3) and inherent authority to dismiss on laches grounds (alleging a 15-month delay timed for litigation advantage) or to stay pending the Underlying Action.
summary.practical_takeaway: Where advancement turns on an "agreed to become" director capacity, a corporation can defeat it by amending the underlying pleading to drop the capacity-based counts, provided the amendment changes the substance rather than the labels; claimants should press the 'by reason of the fact' nexus based on the operative pleading and be prepared to show that the surviving claims depend on the use of corporate powers. Practitioners should also note that amended Rule 56(f) expressly allows summary judgment for a defendant that moves only to dismiss or stay.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 56(a) summary judgment (no genuine dispute of material fact; judgment as a matter of law), with the Court invoking Rule 56(f) and its inherent authority to grant summary judgment for the nonmovant; advancement provisions read by their plain meaning.
